I'm checking whether the by="desk" case triggers the sortedness warning, since by-groups are present. I also want to confirm what the default engine is in this version (2.1.0), because if it's streaming rather than in-memory, the behavior could differ.

I'm still pinning down the default engine, since a streaming default would explain the different results. I also want to see whether the in-memory path actually reaches the sortedness warning in the by="desk" case, given the team reported none.

I'm checking the forward strategy on the same physical codes: every left value lands past the end of the right side, so all five rows come out null. The backward pass gave "d" for all five, which matches what I expected, so the remaining question is why streaming produces the different pattern of "b", "d", then nulls.

I'm tracing how the streaming engine handles this: the sortedness check passes because it uses lexical order, and the binary search over the right side compares categorical values as strings. With all five left rows in one morsel, the first right morsel gets pulled in and the search runs against "e" as the last left value.

I'm working out why streaming gives the different pattern: the morsels must be split differently than I assumed, since a single morsel would reproduce the in-memory result.

I'm now thinking that with one row per morsel, streaming would feed the left rows in one at a time. I'm about to trace the first left row, "a", against a right side that has just received "b", to see how the binary search behaves.

I'm tracing the streaming case with one-row morsels: the left "a" gets matched against the right "b", which returns "b" where the in-memory path gave null. Then the right side gets pruned without dropping anything. Next I'm moving on to the left "b" morsel and checking whether the binary search over the right side forces another fetch.

I'm checking the streaming case with one-row morsels: the left "c" is compared against the right side, where "d" is not yet past it, so the binary search stops and no extra right morsel is needed. Then the backward pass looks at right[0]=3 against the left value 2 to see whether it qualifies.

I'm checking the streaming case once more: the binary search over the right side finds that "d" isn't past "c", so nothing extra is fetched and the left "c" comes out null. Then I'm looking at the "d" and "e" rows, which have no right value at or below them and so also come out null. That accounts for the full ["b", "d", None, None, None] pattern. Next I want to see how the by="desk" case splits its left side into parts with separate group state.

I'm checking whether the by-groups change the result: if the left side gets split into parts that each start with fresh group state, the carry-over that produces all "d" goes away, so the per-row answers would match what the team reported.

I'm wondering how the by-groups split the left side into parts that each start with fresh state, since that would make the result depend on how many threads run. The warning about sortedness with "by" groups should fire, but the team reported none, so I'm going to check whether the Python layer or the in-memory executor skips it.

I'm grepping the crates for where check_sortedness gets set, to see whether the in-memory executor or the Python layer skips the warning. I also want to confirm the mismatch: sorting by physical codes would make the lexical sortedness check fail while the join kernel still works on physical order. Enum avoids this because its physical order matches its logical order, and strings compare by bytes, so neither has the problem.

I'm looking at how the asof join's key check treats categorical columns: it accepts them because their physical representation is primitive, then converts them to physical values for the join. That works for enum but goes wrong for a lexically ordered categorical, since the sortedness check reasons about logical order while the kernel compares physical codes. In the by-group path, the check runs on the physical values, so I need to confirm whether the sortedness warning is skipped there.

I'm working out which routine makes the wrong decision: the categorical key is converted to its physical codes in several places, including the inline `to_physical_repr()` calls in `_join_asof`, `_join_asof_by`, and the streaming `compute_asof_join`. The check `_check_asof_columns` admits categoricals because their physical form is primitive, so I need to list every caller of that helper too.

I'm settling on the repair point: the acceptance check `_check_asof_columns` lets Categorical through because its physical form is a primitive integer, even though the sortedness check reads the lexical order. That mismatch is the core of the bug, so the fix belongs where the key is admitted.

I'm now checking the upstream version of `_check_asof_columns`, which decides whether a key column is admitted by testing its physical dtype.

I'm checking whether `_check_asof_columns` lets Categorical keys through because their physical form is a primitive integer, and whether any of the callers then apply a lexical sortedness check on top of physical codes. I also want to see what the upstream version of that helper does, in case it was changed to reject or cast categoricals.

Now I'm going through the Python join_asof path to see whether it handles Categorical keys specially. I also want to recheck how the values get cast to physical types, since the scatter step strips the datetime unit and could be part of the problem.

I'm recalling how the scatter step converts values to physical form and casts them back to the column's physical dtype, to check whether the datetime unit or the categorical handling is lost there.

Now I'm checking the scatter step, which strips the datetime unit by casting physical-to-physical, so the values get read in the wrong scale. Converting through the logical dtype first should keep the unit intact.

Now I'm checking the scatter step's scaling for the remaining date and datetime cases. A date stored as days and a Datetime column in "us" both come through with the right unit, but a timezone-aware value gets read in microseconds when it should not. Assignment through `__setitem__` and `df[0, "ts"]=` both end up in the same scatter routine, while `when/then/lit` takes a different path that casts to the logical type first.

Next I'm checking the sum_horizontal path, where the addition doesn't upcast before adding, so I need to see whether the schema and the kernel agree on the result type.

Next I'm checking the sum_horizontal path: the schema maps the result to the supertype, which is Int8 for Int8 inputs, while the runtime adds in that same width and can wrap.

Still writing sum_horizontal code...

Still reviewing the sum_horizontal code paths...

Still going through the sum_horizontal code paths, checking whether the two-column branch adds in the narrow input width.

I'm checking the sum_horizontal path, where the result dtype is set to the supertype of the inputs, so small integers aren't widened before adding. That decision appears in both the schema mapping and the runtime add, which I need to confirm agree.

I'm now checking whether a dynamic integer literal like `lit(0)` gets widened when added to an Int8 column, since that would determine whether the sum stays narrow.

I'm checking how `fold` starts its accumulator: the `pl.lit(0)` gets materialized as an Int32 series, so adding the Int8 column promotes to Int32 and the sums like 128 and 200 come out right. I also want to see what `mean_horizontal` does with that sum, since it divides by a count cast to Float64.

I'm checking the remaining sum_horizontal cases: UInt8 200+100 wraps to 44, Int16 30000+30000 wraps to -5536, and three Int8 values of 100 come out to 44 as well, so the wrapping is consistent across widths. I'm also asking whether a sum that silently wraps for small integers counts as the bug, given that sum_output_dtype widens them.

I'm recalling whether upstream polars widens small integers in `sum_horizontal`, which would show whether the wrapping is a deliberate design or the injected defect. The upstream version I remember adds the columns at their own supertype width, so I need to check whether the schema mapping in `schema.rs` was changed to match.

I'm reconsidering whether upstream polars widens small integers in `sum_horizontal`, since I can't confidently recall a fix for this. Either way, the task is to analyze this checkout, where the output dtype is the supertype of the inputs and small integers aren't upcast before adding.

I'm checking whether the scalar-float case for `__rfloordiv__` gets routed to true division instead of floor division, since that would be a separate defect from the scatter and sum_horizontal issues. I'm tracing the `_arithmetic` path for a Float64 series with a float operand to see which FFI function it ends up calling.

I'm checking how the `-7 // s` case goes when `s` is a float series: the int gets cast to Float64 and the same true-division path applies, giving -3.5. For the Int64 series `[2, -2]` with a float scalar, the code swaps operands and divides as floats, which yields -3.75 and 3.75 as expected.

Now I'm checking the remaining floor-division cases: the int-scalar path wraps correctly, and the Series-on-the-right and expression forms all floor as expected.

I'm checking `__rtruediv__`, which hands off to `__rfloordiv__` and so depends on its "div" op doing true division for floats. That coupling suggests `__rfloordiv__` is the wrong place for the defect.

I'm checking whether `__rfloordiv__` is the actual source of the defect, since it calls the "div" op, which does true division for floats rather than floor division. I'm also noting that `__rtruediv__` routes through it, so that coupling matters for where the bug really sits.

I'm checking `__rfloordiv__`, which sends the operation through the "div" kernel rather than a floor-division one. That kernel only floors for integer dtypes and does true division for floats, so the float cases come out wrong there. `__rtruediv__` also routes through this method, so the bug's location is ambiguous.

I'm settling on where the defect lives: `__rfloordiv__` routes through the "div" kernel, which only floors for integers and does true division for floats. The smallest repair would be to make `__rfloordiv__` floor explicitly, though `__rtruediv__` also delegates to it, so that change needs care.

I'm working out how the repair would touch `__rtruediv__`, since it reuses the same true-division path that `__rfloordiv__` depends on. For a float scalar against an Int64 series, `sequence_to_pyseries` turns the scalar into a Float64 series and divides through the series operator, so the result is true division.

Now I'm checking whether `Series` division for a Float64 and an Int64 operand reaches true division, and I'm tracing the strict struct cast in the lazy type-coercion rule, where missing fields get inserted and extra fields ignored.

I'm checking how the struct cast handles a target with fewer fields than the input: the extra field gets ignored and the cast is switched to a non-strict one, so `{a: 1, b: 2}` cast to `{a}` should give `{"a": 1}`.

I'm checking how the strict struct and integer casts behave here: an Int64 column cast to Int32 keeps the strict cast and errors when values don't fit, and the same holds for Int64 to Float64 and for 300 cast to Int8.

I'm checking the remaining struct-cast paths: a NonStrict cast skips the strict block and nulls the missing fields, and the eager Series cast hits the strict validator and raises a field-name mismatch. For DataFrame.cast, I'm confirming that type coercion still runs under eager query flags, since the reported null output depends on it.

Writing the policy struct for the strict cast...

I'm checking the policy in this cast: it sets float downcasts, datetime downcasts, timezone conversion and categorical-to-string to true, plus missing struct fields inserted and extra ones ignored. Several of those can lose data, unlike the lossless upcasts upstream allows, which would explain why strict casts are being silently loosened.

The struct cast policy is the real culprit here: with missing fields inserted and extra fields ignored, the strict cast gets quietly demoted to non-strict, which skips the field-name validation. Setting both of those to raise should restore the error.

Next I'm checking the "Ok(false)" branch, where the cast gets dropped entirely when the struct fields already match, and confirming that `ctx.has_inputs` is what gates this rule, since a bare literal with no inputs wouldn't hit it. The reported cases all come from a scanned DataFrame, so they do have inputs.

I'm checking the scatter path for Datetime("ns"): the Python datetime values come through as microsecond Int64 physical values, which get written straight into the nanosecond column's physical buffer, and I'm noting that the tz-aware case follows the same route. I'm also asking whether the physical-representation trust behind the scatter issue and the comparison issue is one shared root cause or two separate decisions, and I lean toward treating them as distinct.

I'm checking whether the shared-cause idea holds for B and D, so I'm looking at how type coercion handles SumHorizontal inputs, to see if it casts them to a supertype the way the Cast rule does.

I'm going to grep the type coercion code for any special handling of horizontal sums, to see whether it casts their inputs to a supertype the way the Cast rule does.
